title: Seedling ozone sensitivity did not predict growth or mortality differences among 12 mature tree species in 16 eastern US states in 1999-2025, but the test cannot exclude a seedling-size growth loss
abstract: Question: do the EPA seedling ozone exposure-response functions (Lee et al. 2022, W126) predict which mature forest trees grew less or died more where and when ozone exposure was high? Data: USDA FIA remeasurements in 16 eastern US states (14,646 plots; 742,662 growth and 868,290 mortality intervals, trees >= 12.7 cm DBH, 1999-2025); W126 from EPA AQS hourly ozone (our 2010-2024 monitor table plus the 1999-2009 table of sci:268004a0), interpolated to plots; nClimGrid weather and TDep deposition controls. The plan was frozen and timestamped before the outcome data were read. Method: predicted seedling biomass loss (PRBL) of each species at its interval W126 was compared between species in the same plot and visit (plot-visit fixed effects, species-specific size, climate and deposition terms); the translation ratio lambda is the share of seedling loss seen in adult diameter growth; inference by 2,000 species-label permutations. Results: lambda = -0.37 (95% CI -1.88 to 1.14), permutation p = 0.68; the same in eight robustness subsets. The test has low power: the permutation null of lambda spans -1.36 to 1.38, and the power for lambda = 1 is 0.41. Black cherry had the expected ozone slope, tulip poplar the opposite sign. Mortality did not increase with predicted loss (permutation p = 0.78). The predicted ozone x moisture interaction had the expected sign (-0.86, SE 0.39) but permutation p = 0.12, and a moisture-tercile split gave the opposite pattern. Models within the same tree over time were confounded by species time trends (permutation null median equal to the estimate). Limitations: species-level confounding sets the detection limit; ozone decreased mostly with time; diameter growth only; no western species.
